questions.q: What is the primary source of funds that commercial banks use to provide loans to businesses and individuals?
questions.a: The primary source of funds is the deposits made by savers into savings, current, and fixed accounts at the bank. If a student answers "government grants" or "bank owner's personal wealth," it reveals a misunderstanding of how financial intermediation works, thinking banks operate purely on external funding rather than pooling community savings.

questions.q: Why do banks charge a higher interest rate on loans they give out compared to the interest rate they pay to people who deposit savings?
questions.a: Banks charge higher interest on loans (lending rate) than they pay on deposits (borrowing/saving rate) to cover their operational costs, administrative expenses, risk of default, and to make a profit. A student who believes banks charge the same interest rate fails to understand the profit model of financial intermediaries, missing how the "interest spread" keeps banks in business.

questions.q: A farmer takes a crop loan of ₹40,000 from a commercial bank for one year at an annual simple interest rate of 8%. Calculate the total amount the farmer must repay to the bank at the end of the year.
questions.a:
Step 1: Identify given values: Principal (P) = ₹40,000, Rate (R) = 8% per annum, Time (T) = 1 year.
Step 2: Recall simple interest formula: Interest = $(P \times R \times T) / 100$.
Step 3: Calculate interest: $(40,000 \times 8 \times 1) / 100 = ₹3,200$.
Step 4: Calculate total repayment amount: Principal + Interest = $₹40,000 + ₹3,200 = ₹43,200$.
A student who answers only ₹3,200 has calculated just the interest without adding back the original principal, forgetting that a loan must be repaid in full plus the cost of borrowing.

questions.q: Analyze what happens to economic activity in a town if a commercial bank suddenly stops granting credit to local shopkeepers and farmers.
questions.a: Stopping credit restricts local businesses from expanding inventory or purchasing seeds and equipment, leading to lower production, fewer jobs, and a slowdown in local market exchange. A student who thinks the local economy will remain unaffected ignores the crucial role that credit plays in funding productive investments and daily commerce.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Taking a bank loan is always harmful because you end up paying more money back than you borrowed." Is this economically accurate for all types of loans?
questions.a: This is economically inaccurate because loans used for productive investments (like buying machinery or expanding a shop) generate higher revenue and profits that far outweigh the cost of interest. A student who agrees entirely views loans solely as a consumer burden, failing to distinguish between unproductive debt and productive credit that builds wealth.

questions.q: Propose a simple three-step plan for a small vegetable vendor who wants to secure a bank loan of ₹10,000 to buy a larger pushcart and weighing scale.
questions.a: The plan should include: 1) Opening a savings bank account and maintaining a steady transaction record; 2) Preparing a simple business plan showing how the new pushcart will increase daily sales and income; 3) Submitting required identity documents and proof of business to the bank officer. A poor answer might suggest asking strangers or ignoring bank requirements, showing a lack of understanding of formal credit systems.
